claim: Biofilms are bacterial communities of cells encased by a self-produced matrix.
source: Biofilms, bacterial communities of cells encased by a self-produced matrix, exhibit a variety of three-dimensional structures.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract that establishes what biofilms are.

claim: Channel networks formed within the bulk of the biofilm play an important role in the colonies' viability by promoting the transport of nutrients and chemicals.
source: Specifically, channel networks formed within the bulk of the biofilm have been identified to play an important role in the colonies' viability by promoting the transport of nutrients and chemicals.
evidence: This statement references prior identification of channel networks' role, implying citation to existing literature.

claim: The formation of wrinkles and folds in P. aeruginosa biofilms is triggered by a mechanical buckling instability.
source: The formation of the wrinkles and folds is triggered by a mechanical buckling instability, controlled by biofilm growth rate and the film's adhesion to the substrate.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on the experimental work presented.

claim: The mechanical buckling instability is controlled by biofilm growth rate and the film's adhesion to the substrate.
source: The formation of the wrinkles and folds is triggered by a mechanical buckling instability, controlled by biofilm growth rate and the film's adhesion to the substrate.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Three-dimensional folding gives rise to hollow channels that rapidly increase the effective volume occupied by the biofilm.
source: The three-dimensional folding gives rise to hollow channels that rapidly increase the effective volume occupied by the biofilm and facilitate bacterial movement inside them.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Hollow channels facilitate bacterial movement inside them.
source: The three-dimensional folding gives rise to hollow channels that rapidly increase the effective volume occupied by the biofilm and facilitate bacterial movement inside them.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Bacteria predominantly exist in biofilms.
source: Bacteria predominantly exist in biofilms, surface-attached aggregates of cells (Nadell et al., 2017; Flemming et al., 2016; Flemming and Wuertz, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In biofilms, cells are enclosed in autoproduced, strongly hydrated extracellular polymeric substances (EPS).
source: In biofilms, the cells are enclosed in autoproduced, strongly hydrated extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), which form the extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about biofilm structure based on established knowledge.

claim: The EPS consists of polysaccharides, proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids.
source: The EPS consists of polysaccharides, the most abundant component, proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids (Lasa, 2006; Frølund et al., 1996; Flemming and Wingender, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Polysaccharides are the most abundant component of the EPS.
source: The EPS consists of polysaccharides, the most abundant component, proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids (Lasa, 2006; Frølund et al., 1996; Flemming and Wingender, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The viscoelastic nature of the matrix provides mechanical stability to the biofilm.
source: The matrix plays different roles: its viscoelastic nature provides mechanical stability to the biofilm, while its physical chemistry is responsible for the adhesion to the surface and internal cohesion (Costerton et al., 1987; Hall-Stoodley et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The physical chemistry of the matrix is responsible for adhesion to the surface and internal cohesion.
source: The matrix plays different roles: its viscoelastic nature provides mechanical stability to the biofilm, while its physical chemistry is responsible for the adhesion to the surface and internal cohesion (Costerton et al., 1987; Hall-Stoodley et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The matrix's structural properties contribute to the exceptional viability of the bacterial community in the biofilm lifestyle.
source: Additionally, not only mechanical and chemical but also the matrix's structural properties contribute to the exceptional viability of the bacterial community in the biofilm lifestyle (Epstein et al., 2011; Okegbe et al., 2014; Madsen et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mechanistic understanding of how environmental conditions and surface characteristics affect biofilm structure is still limited.
source: However, the mechanistic understanding of how environmental conditions and the characteristics of the surfaces on which they grow affect the biofilm structure is still limited.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Hydrodynamic conditions control mass transfer in biofilms.
source: Hydrodynamic conditions control mass transfer, which in turn controls the transport of nutrients, metabolic products, and signal molecules (Purevdorj et al., 2002; Krsmanovic et al., 2021; Conrad and Poling-Skutvik, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Fluid flow exerts drag forces on the biofilm and shapes its structure.
source: Fluid flow also exerts drag forces on the biofilm and shapes its structure (Stoodley et al., 1998; Stoodley et al., 1999; Pearce et al., 2019; Hartmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Under strong flows, bacteria often form biofilm streamers in the shape of long, filamentous structures.
source: Under strong flows, bacteria often form biofilm streamers in the shape of long, filamentous structures; while, under weak flow conditions, some bacteria form surface-attached colonies with ripple-like structures (Rusconi et al., 2011; Rusconi et al., 2010; Purevdorj et al., 2002; Drescher et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Under weak flow conditions, some bacteria form surface-attached colonies with ripple-like structures.
source: Under strong flows, bacteria often form biofilm streamers in the shape of long, filamentous structures; while, under weak flow conditions, some bacteria form surface-attached colonies with ripple-like structures (Rusconi et al., 2011; Rusconi et al., 2010; Purevdorj et al., 2002; Drescher et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some biofilms exhibit three-dimensional morphologies characterized by the presence of folds and wrinkles.
source: Some biofilms exhibit three-dimensional morphologies characterized by the presence of folds and wrinkles that have been proposed to improve the viability of the biofilm due to improved uptake and transport of oxygen and nutrients (Wilking et al., 2012; Kempes et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Folds and wrinkles have been proposed to improve biofilm viability due to improved uptake and transport of oxygen and nutrients.
source: Some biofilms exhibit three-dimensional morphologies characterized by the presence of folds and wrinkles that have been proposed to improve the viability of the biofilm due to improved uptake and transport of oxygen and nutrients (Wilking et al., 2012; Kempes et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Biofilm grown on agar induces additional complexities as biological and mechanical contributions are tightly interconnected.
source: However, a biofilm grown on agar induces additional complexities, as biological and mechanical contributions are tightly interconnected.
evidence: This is an assessment based on the authors' understanding of biofilm-agar systems.

claim: Biofilms grown on agar are characterized by substantial heterogeneity in nutrient availability.
source: Biofilms grown on agar are characterized by substantial heterogeneity in nutrient availability, generated by the diffusive nature of nutrient transport within the agar, which leads to differences in growth rates and subsequent mechanical stresses across the biofilm (Stewart, 2003; Wilking et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Anisotropic growth may be the driving force for folding in colonies with moderate adhesion to substrates.
source: Theoretical and experimental studies found that, in particular, an anisotropic growth may be the driving force for folding in colonies with moderate adhesion to the substrates (Ben Amar and Wu, 2014; Espeso et al., 2015; Fei et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bacterial cells first grow as a uniform layer of increasing thickness on the PDMS.
source: Bacterial cells exposed to the flow of nutrients first grow as a uniform layer of increasing thickness on the PDMS.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: No significant biofilm formation is observed on the glass within the timeframe of the experiments.
source: No significant biofilm formation is observed on the glass within the timeframe of our experiments.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: The presence of wrinkles and voids increases the effective average thickness of the biofilm.
source: It can be noted that the presence of wrinkles and voids increases the effective average thickness of the biofilm.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: The temporal evolution of the structure can be divided into three distinct stages.
source: The temporal evolution of the structure can be divided into three distinct stages.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: The first stage starts shortly before the first wrinkles appear at 49 hr after the start of nutrient flow and lasts 6.5 hr.
source: The first stage starts shortly before the first wrinkles appear, which is 49 hr after the start of the nutrient flow, and lasts 6.5 hr.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of experimental observations.

claim: In the second phase, which lasts approximately 3.5 hr, the number of isolated wrinkles decreases because they start to merge and form longer, interconnected paths.
source: In the second phase, which lasts approximately 3.5 hr, the number of isolated wrinkles decreases because they start to merge and form longer, interconnected paths.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of experimental observations.

claim: In the third phase, the biofilm structure reaches a steady state where the longest wrinkle does not grow in length anymore.
source: Finally, in the third phase, the biofilm structure reaches a steady state where the longest wrinkle does not grow in length anymore and the number of unconnected wrinkles stays consistently low.
evidence: This is a description of experimental observations.

claim: The final stage has been observed to last at least 5 hr.
source: This final stage has been observed to last at least 5 hr, while the whole process of biofilm wrinkling proceeds over 9–10 hr once the first wrinkles appear and until a steady state is reached.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of experimental observations.

claim: The whole process of biofilm wrinkling proceeds over 9-10 hr once the first wrinkles appear until a steady state is reached.
source: This final stage has been observed to last at least 5 hr, while the whole process of biofilm wrinkling proceeds over 9–10 hr once the first wrinkles appear and until a steady state is reached.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of experimental observations.

claim: The wrinkles consist of hollow channels that detach from the substrate during their formation.
source: The wrinkles consist of hollow channels that detach from the substrate during their formation.
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy experiments.

claim: The center of the wrinkle does not show a fluorescent signal and is therefore devoid of any biofilm matrix.
source: In contrast, the center of the wrinkle does not show a fluorescent signal and is therefore devoid of any biofilm matrix.
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy with fluorescent staining.

claim: The channel height is substantially greater than the thickness of the original biofilm layer.
source: A vertical slice through a confocal volume along the x-z-plane (Figure 2c) shows that the channel height is substantially greater than the thickness of the original biofilm layer.
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy.

claim: No biofilm matrix was detected on the PDMS substrate at the location of the channel.
source: Furthermore, no biofilm matrix was detected on the PDMS substrate at the location of the channel.
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy.

claim: The biofilm fully detaches from the substrate during channel formation.
source: This indicates that the biofilm fully detaches from the substrate, similar to our analogy where the fabric separates from the substrate to form a pattern of wrinkles and folds.
evidence: This is an inference from the microscopy observations.

claim: Buckling-delamination is the underlying mechanism driving the formation of a channel network throughout the biofilm.
source: This delamination between the biofilm and the PDMS substrate allows us to identify buckling-delamination as the underlying mechanism driving the formation of a channel network throughout the biofilm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The growth of the biofilm in a confined environment acts as the driving force for the buckling instability.
source: The growth of the biofilm in a confined environment acts as the driving force for the buckling instability, which leads to the formation of the channel network.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the nutrient on/off experiment.

claim: Channel formation restarts when the nutrient solution is reintroduced in the microfluidic channel.
source: The channel formation restarts as the nutrient solution is reintroduced in the microfluidic channel and continues, as shown in Figure 3a (right panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the nutrient on/off experiment shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Biofilm growth is the key driving force for the formation of a channel network.
source: Therefore, we can unambiguously identify biofilm growth as the key driving force for the formation of a channel network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the nutrient on/off experiment.

claim: P. aeruginosa biofilms are capable of exerting stresses in the kPa-range during growth.
source: Previous experimental studies have reported that P. aeruginosa biofilms are indeed capable of exerting stresses in the kPa-range during growth (Chew et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The biofilm grown on low surface free energy PDMS undergoes clear buckling-delamination and develops a channel network.
source: The biofilm grown on low surface free energy PDMS (left) undergoes clear buckling-delamination and develops a channel network.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments comparing different PDMS surfaces.

claim: The biofilm grown on high surface free energy PDMS does not undergo buckling-delamination and remains homogeneously adherent to the PDMS substrate.
source: The biofilm grown on high surface free energy PDMS (right) does not undergo buckling-delamination and remains homogeneously adherent to the PDMS substrate.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments comparing different PDMS surfaces.

claim: Channel formation can be suppressed by increasing the surface free energy of the substrate.
source: These results show that channel formation can be suppressed by increasing the surface free energy of the substrate and, consequently, the adhesion strength between the biofilm and the substrate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments comparing different PDMS surfaces.

claim: As a channel network is formed, the average biofilm thickness increases substantially and at a greater rate compared to a biofilm where no channels are formed.
source: In the next step, we monitor the effective biofilm thickness measured from the PDMS surface to the top of the biofilm layer over time and find that, as a channel network is formed, the average biofilm thickness increases substantially and at a greater rate compared to a biofilm where no channels are formed.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments comparing biofilms on different PDMS surfaces.

claim: The increase in effective thickness during channel formation does not necessarily correspond to an increase in growth rate or biomass compared to the non-buckled biofilm.
source: The illustrations in Figure 4b clarify that the increase in effective thickness during channel formation does not necessarily correspond to an increase in growth rate or biomass compared to the non-buckled biofilm, as water-filled channels primarily constitute the additional volume.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: The biofilm morphology can be controlled locally by solely adjusting the surface free energy of the substrate with a spatial resolution in the millimeter range.
source: The biofilm morphology can be controlled locally by solely adjusting the surface free energy of the substrate with a spatial resolution in the millimeter range (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the patterned PDMS experiment shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The morphological change is as abrupt as the change in surface free energy.
source: Remarkably, the morphological change is as abrupt as the change in surface free energy.
evidence: This is an observation from the patterned PDMS experiment.

claim: The channel network is devoid of any biofilm matrix and densely populated by actively motile bacteria.
source: The channel network is devoid of any biofilm matrix and densely populated by actively motile bacteria, as shown by the movie of bacteria swimming in a channel Figure 5—video 1.
evidence: This is an observation from high-speed microscopy with reference to video data.

claim: The bacterial motion shows no preferential direction.
source: The bacterial motion shows no preferential direction, and high-speed images can be used to calculate a spatially resolved time-correlation coefficient (Secchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from high-speed microscopy.

claim: Active areas with detectable bacteria movement are highly localized and distinct from inactive areas.
source: It becomes clear that areas with detectable bacteria movement are highly localized and distinct from inactive areas.
evidence: This is an observation from the activity map analysis.

claim: The active areas are exclusively found inside the channels of the biofilm.
source: A comparison between the activity map and the biofilm microstructure, as shown in the bright-field micrographs, reveals that the active areas are exclusively found inside the channels of the biofilm.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing activity maps with brightfield images.

claim: The hollow channel network gets populated by motile bacteria as the channels form.
source: These results indicate that the hollow channel network gets populated by motile bacteria as the channels form.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the activity map analysis.

claim: As the biofilm matures, the bacterial activity diminishes until it can not be detected anymore.
source: As the biofilm matures, the bacterial activity diminishes until it can not be detected anymore (Figure 5a, right panel), without any structural changes in the biofilm.
evidence: This is an observation from the activity map analysis over time.

claim: The decrease in bacterial motility comes without a dispersal event nor deformation or structural changes of the biofilm.
source: The corresponding phase-contrast image reveals that the decrease in bacterial motility comes without a dispersal event nor deformation or structural changes of the biofilm.
evidence: This is an observation from phase-contrast microscopy.

claim: The decrease in bacterial motility is attributable to a renewed surface colonization and subsequent biofilm formation of the planktonic cells in the channels.
source: We hypothesize that this decrease in bacterial motility is attributable to a renewed surface colonization and subsequent biofilm formation of the planktonic cells in the channels.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the observations.

claim: The swimming speed of the motile bacteria inside the channel network is not affected by the fluid flow surrounding the biofilm.
source: The swimming speed of the motile bacteria inside the channel network is not affected by the fluid flow surrounding the biofilm.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the DDM experiments at different flow rates.

claim: The average bacterial swimming speed was measured as a function of the mean flow rates of the nutrient solution surrounding the biofilm.
source: The average bacterial swimming speed was measured as a function of the mean flow rates of the nutrient solution surrounding the biofilm.
evidence: This is a description of the DDM experiment.

claim: The bulk flow surrounding the biofilm does not introduce advection inside the biofilm.
source: These findings indicate that the bulk flow surrounding the biofilm does not introduce advection inside the biofilm, and therefore the channels consist of a closed biofilm matrix layer populated by motile bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DDM experiments.

claim: The channels consist of a closed biofilm matrix layer populated by motile bacteria.
source: These findings indicate that the bulk flow surrounding the biofilm does not introduce advection inside the biofilm, and therefore the channels consist of a closed biofilm matrix layer populated by motile bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DDM experiments.

claim: A buckling-delamination process governs the formation of three-dimensional hollow channels.
source: A buckling-delamination process governs the formation of three-dimensional hollow channels.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The biofilm morphology is determined by the isotropic growth of the biofilm in a confined space and the adhesion between the biofilm and the solid substrate.
source: Experimentally, we show that the biofilm morphology is determined by the isotropic growth of the biofilm in a confined space and the adhesion between the biofilm and the solid substrate.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The introduction of moderate fluid flow increases nutrient flux at the surface of the biofilm and therefore minimizes nutrient gradients in the bulk of thin biofilms.
source: In our case, the introduction of moderate fluid flow increases nutrient flux at the surface of the biofilm and therefore minimizes nutrient gradients in the bulk of thin biofilms (Krsmanovic et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental system with citation to prior literature.

claim: In the simple system of confined growth of a uniform biofilm, compressive stresses are high enough to induce buckling and channel formation.
source: These findings also show that in the simple system of confined growth of a uniform biofilm, compressive stresses are high enough to induce buckling and channel formation, a result that has recently been seen in bacterial pellicles by Qin et al., 2021.
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study with reference to similar findings in other systems.

claim: The biofilm delaminates and buckles away from the substrate to form a channel network.
source: In our system, the biofilm delaminates and buckles away from the substrate to form a channel network.
evidence: This is a description of the observed mechanism.

claim: An increase in adhesive strength between the biofilm and the substrate impedes channel formation.
source: Additionally, we showed experimentally that an increase in adhesive strength between the biofilm and the substrate impedes channel formation, as the biofilm can no longer delaminate.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments with different PDMS surfaces.

claim: The findings are general and applicable to other bacterial species.
source: Furthermore, we hypothesize that our findings are general and applicable to other bacterial species as our growth conditions - fluid flow and the presence of solid substrates – are often found in the biofilms habitats.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: The overnight culture was diluted 1:100 in tryptone broth and grown for 2 hr until OD600 reached 0.2.
source: The overnight culture was then diluted 1:100 in tryptone broth (TB) and grown for 2 hr until OD600 reached the value of 0.2.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: The bacterial suspension was diluted 1:10 and used to inoculate the microfluidic channel.
source: The bacterial suspension was then diluted 1:10 and used to inoculate the microfluidic channel.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: The bacteria were left undisturbed for 1 hr before fresh media was flown using the syringe pump.
source: The bacteria were left undisturbed for 1 hr before fresh media was flown using the syringe pump.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: Rectangular microfluidic channels were fabricated using standard soft lithography techniques.
source: Rectangular microfluidic channels were fabricated using standard soft lithography techniques (Xia and Whitesides, 1998).
evidence: This is a description of the fabrication method with citation.

claim: Hydrophilic PDMS with 0.5% dimethylsiloxan-ethyleneoxide blockcopolymer was produced according to Gökaltun et al., 2019.
source: Hydrophilic PDMS with 0.5% dimethylsiloxan-ethyleneoxide blockcopolymer (DBE-712, Gelest, Morrisville, PA) was produced according to Gökaltun et al., 2019.
evidence: This is a description of the material preparation with citation.

claim: The surface free energies of the hydrophilic and hydrophobic PDMS were determined with the Owens-Wendt-Method.
source: The surface free energies of the hydrophilic and hydrophic PDMS were determined with the Owens-Wendt-Method (Owens and Wendt, 1969), where the contact angles of known liquids with the substrate are used to determine the unknown surface free energy of the substrate.
evidence: This is a description of the measurement method with citation.

claim: Propidium iodide staining was performed to measure the thickness of the biofilm.
source: Staining with a propidium iodide solution was performed to measure the thickness of the biofilm.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: GFP-labelled Concanavalin A was used to visualize the three-dimensional structure.
source: GFP-labelled Concanavalin A (Sigma Aldrich) was used to visualize the three-dimensional structure.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: Light microscopy images were taken on Nikon Eclipse Ti2-A in phase-contrast configuration.
source: Light microscopy images were taken on Nikon Eclipse Ti2-A in phase-contrast configuration, equipped with a Hamamatsu ImageEM-X2 CCD camera and a 20 x objective.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging equipment and method.

claim: For fluorescent visualizations, a Nikon Eclipes T1 inverted microscope coupled with a Yokogawa CSU-W1-T2 confocal scanner unit was used.
source: For the fluorescent visualizations, we used a Nikon Eclipes T1 inverted microscope coupled with a Yokogawa CSU-W1-T2 confocal scanner unit and equipped with an Andor iXon Ultra EMCCD camera.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging equipment.

claim: Images were acquired at 2000 frames per second with the Fastcam UX100 high-speed camera for DDM.
source: Images were acquired at 2000 frames per second with the Fastcam UX100 (Photron, Japan) high-speed camera on the Nikon Eclipse Ti2-A microscope in brightfield mode.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging method for DDM.

claim: DDM was performed according to Cerbino and Trappe, 2008 using a custom code written in Matlab.
source: Differential Dynamic Microscopy (DDM) was performed according to Cerbino and Trappe, 2008 using a custom code written in Matlab.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method with citation.

claim: Images were acquired at 1000 frames per second for spatially resolved correlation analysis.
source: Images were acquired at 1000 frames per second with the Fastcam UX100 (Photron, Japan) high-speed camera on the Nikon Eclipse Ti2-A microscope in brightfield mode.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging method for correlation analysis.
